strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation addressing practical shortcomings of existing visual floorplan localization methods (such as F3Loc), specifically the absence of uncertainty modeling and poor cross-environment generalization.

Sound and elegant probabilistic formulation: modeling floorplan depth with an explicit Laplace distribution enables natural heteroscedastic uncertainty estimation and seamless integration into the Bayes/histogram filter observation model.

Convincing and thorough experimental evaluation on both synthetic (Gibson, Structured3D) and challenging real-world datasets (LaMAR HGE/CAB), showing large improvements over prior work, especially on short sequences and unseen environments.

Comprehensive ablation study that dissects the contributions of the modern monodepth backbone versus the uncertainty modeling, as well as comparisons across multiple foundation model backbones (Depth Anything V2 variants, DepthPro, DINOv2).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is relatively incremental over F3Loc (Chen et al., CVPR 2024), essentially combining the F3Loc architecture and histogram filter pipeline with an off-the-shelf foundation depth encoder and standard heteroscedastic Laplace NLL uncertainty modeling.

Although the depth encoder is off-the-shelf, the downstream masked attention and prediction heads still require domain-specific training on floorplan depth pairs, which slightly tempers the claim of fully eliminating per-environment training.

Inference latency is significantly higher than F3Loc (feature extraction takes ~0.18s vs ~0.015s for F3Loc on Gibson, and matching on large floorplans takes ~0.8s), making high-frequency mobile deployment challenging without the proposed frame-skipping / grid-coarsening approximations.

strengths: Addresses key practical limitations of existing visual floorplan localization methods (such as F3Loc), specifically the vulnerability to depth estimation failures in complex geometry and the poor generalization of dataset-specific depth networks.

Formulating the floorplan observation likelihood via an explicit heteroscedastic Laplace distribution is geometrically sensible, well-motivated, and integrates seamlessly into the Bayesian histogram filter framework.

Extensive experimental evaluation across synthetic (Gibson, Structured3D) and real-world (LaMAR HGE and cross-domain CAB) datasets, achieving dramatic performance improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods, particularly on short trajectories (e.g., 16.7-fold increase in success rate at T=15 on LaMAR).

Thorough ablations isolating the contributions of foundation depth encoders (comparing Depth Anything V2, DepthPro, and DINOv2 across different scales) versus uncertainty prediction, as well as runtime vs. accuracy trade-offs regarding grid resolution and observation update rates.
Well-written manuscript with clear figures and intuitive qualitative likelihood visualizations.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the core architecture (gravity alignment, masked attention query mechanism, decoupled histogram filter) closely follows the pipeline established by F3Loc, primarily swapping the encoder for off-the-shelf foundation depth models and predicting an additional variance head trained with negative log-likelihood.

Inference latency is considerably higher than custom lightweight networks (e.g., feature extraction takes ~0.18s vs. 0.015s for F3Loc mono), which may pose constraints for resource-constrained robotics or real-time mobile AR platforms.

The evaluation on the challenging real-world dataset (LaMAR HGE / CAB) involves a relatively small number of test trajectories (e.g., N=11 for T=100 on HGE, and N=2 for T=100 on CAB in the supplementary material), which makes the statistical significance of some long-sequence metrics somewhat limited.

The system relies heavily on accurate relative ego-motion (odometry) inputs; the sensitivity and robustness of the histogram filter under significant odometry drift or noise are not explicitly analyzed.

strengths: Sound and well-motivated framework: Extending the visual floorplan localization pipeline with explicit depth uncertainty modeling (using a heteroscedastic Laplace distribution) is theoretically well-grounded and directly integrates into the observation model of the histogram filter.

Strong and convincing empirical improvements: The proposed method substantially outperforms the current state of the art (F3Loc) across synthetic (Gibson, Structured3D) and real-world (LaMAR HGE and CAB) benchmarks, achieving particularly remarkable gains in low-frame regimes (e.g., 20.0% vs. 1.2% SR@1m on LaMAR at T=15).

Thorough ablation studies: The paper cleanly disentangles the benefit of foundation model features from the uncertainty estimation (Tables 1, 2, and 6), demonstrating that uncertainty estimation provides consistent, orthogonal gains across various encoder sizes and architectures.

Comprehensive practical analysis: The submission and supplementary material evaluate real-world trade-offs, including frame-processing runtimes, observation update frequency, and grid cell resolutions.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual and architectural novelty: The overall pipeline heavily builds upon F3Loc (gravity alignment, masked attention query-key matching, 3D histogram filtering). The addition of an uncertainty branch trained via negative log-likelihood of a Laplace distribution is standard practice in heteroscedastic regression.

Confounding impact of modern foundation backbones: A large portion of the performance boost stems from replacing F3Loc's task-specific ResNet encoder with large modern depth foundation models (e.g., Depth Anything V2, DepthPro). While leveraging pre-trained representations is practically justified, it represents an engineering enhancement rather than a novel localization principle.

Limited trajectory sample sizes on real-world splits: In several benchmark configurations on LaMAR HGE and CAB, the number of evaluated sequences for long trajectories is quite small (e.g., N=11 for T=100 in Table 2, and N=2 for T=100 in Table 7), which weakens the statistical reliability of the reported success rates on those specific sequence lengths.

Comparisons with non-filtering / alternative baselines: The comparative evaluation is primarily conducted against variants of F3Loc, while other floorplan localization methods (e.g., LASER, PF-Net, LaLaLoc++) are only included via numbers transcribed from previous publications on limited settings.

strengths: The paper addresses practical and critical failure modes of existing floorplan localization methods (specifically F3Loc): the vulnerability to depth errors in ambiguous indoor regions (e.g., glass, doors, featureless walls) and the reliance on training depth estimators from scratch.

The formulation of aleatoric uncertainty via independent Laplace distributions is well-justified for indoor depth prediction, offering heavy-tailed robustness to large outliers during histogram filtering and post-processing trajectory refinement.

The empirical gains are substantial and convincing, especially on short sequences (e.g., T=15, 20) where time-to-localize is critical for real-world robotics and AR applications, as well as on challenging real-world data (LaMAR HGE and CAB).

The ablation studies are thorough and informative, analyzing backbones (DINOv2, DepthPro, Depth Anything v2 variants), error distributions (Laplace vs. Gaussian), update frequency, grid resolution, and post-processing contributions.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core framework builds closely upon F3Loc (Chen et al., CVPR 2024), integrating established off-the-shelf foundation depth models (Depth Anything v2) and standard heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty regression (Kendall & Gal, 2017) adapted to a Laplace distribution.

The claim that the method 'eliminates the need to rely on per-environment-trained depth networks' is somewhat overstated. While the visual encoder is an off-the-shelf pre-trained model, the masked attention head that maps encoder features to 1D floorplan depth and uncertainty still requires supervised training on floorplan raycast depth data. As shown in the cross-environment evaluation (Tables 4, 7, and 8), fine-tuning on target environments remains necessary to achieve high accuracy.

Matching latency on large floorplans (such as LaMAR HGE) remains high (~0.88s per frame for matching alone on a 0.1m grid), which limits real-time high-framerate deployment without downsampling the grid or reducing observation updates.

strengths: The paper is very well-written, clearly motivated, and addresses two clear limitations of prior state of the art (F3Loc): the lack of uncertainty modeling in depth predictions and the reliance on custom, dataset-specific depth models.

Formulating floorplan depth predictions as Laplace distributions with learned scale parameters is mathematically sound and cleanly integrates into both the histogram filter observation likelihood and the post-processing SE(2) optimization.

The empirical evaluation is thorough and compelling across both synthetic (Gibson) and challenging real-world (LaMAR HGE, LaMAR CAB) datasets, showing massive improvements—especially on short sequences where fast localization convergence is crucial for practical applications.

The ablation studies are comprehensive, systematically isolating the contributions of pre-trained encoders (Depth Anything v2 vs. DepthPro vs. DINOv2), uncertainty modeling, post-processing refinement, observation distribution choices (Laplace vs. Gaussian), and grid resolution/update frequency trade-offs.
weaknesses: The method is an evolutionary extension of F3Loc (Chen et al., CVPR 2024); the core architecture (gravity alignment homography, 1D ray-based masked attention, decoupled histogram filtering) is largely inherited from prior work.

While the visual backbone utilizes pre-trained monocular depth representations, the masked attention head and uncertainty regression heads still require supervised training with raycast floorplan depth ground truth, meaning the overall pipeline is not fully zero-shot for novel layouts.

In the real-world cross-building generalization experiment on LaMAR CAB (Tables 4, 7), the number of test trajectories for long sequences is quite limited (e.g., N=2 for T=100, N=5 for T=50), making the high success rates on long sequences statistically less robust.

strengths: Substantial empirical performance gains over the prior state of the art (F3Loc), particularly in the short-sequence regime (e.g., boosting success rate from 28.4% to 81.3% on Gibson at T=15, and from 1.2% to 50.6% on LaMAR HGE at T=15), which is crucial for practical, fast initialization.

Principled and well-formulated uncertainty integration: modeling floorplan depth as a Laplace distribution directly aligns with the observation likelihood in the Bayesian histogram filter and provides robust weighting for the SE(2) post-processing trajectory optimization.
Thorough experimental validation across both synthetic (Gibson, Structured3D) and real-world (LaMAR HGE and cross-domain LaMAR CAB) datasets.

Detailed and rigorous ablations that cleanly dissect the performance contributions: isolating backbone improvements (+Depth Anything v2) from uncertainty modeling (+Uncertainty), evaluating Laplace vs. Gaussian likelihood formulations (Table 11), comparing different foundation backbones (Table 5), and assessing runtime trade-offs with grid resolution and update frequencies (Tables 9 and 10).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is relatively incremental: the overarching localization pipeline (gravity alignment, masked 1D cross-attention for floorplan depth, ray matching, and histogram filtering) is largely inherited directly from F3Loc (Chen et al., CVPR 2024). The main algorithmic additions—predicting aleatoric uncertainty via Laplace negative log-likelihood and plugging in pre-trained monocular depth models—are well-established techniques in computer vision.

A noticeable fraction of the baseline improvement stems directly from upgrading the feature extractor to Depth Anything v2 rather than algorithmic innovations (e.g., on Gibson at T=100, F3Loc mono jumps from 86.5% to 94.6% purely from the backbone swap), although the authors deserve credit for explicitly ablating this.

The post-processing step contributes significantly to the short-sequence performance boost (e.g., +16 points at T=15 on Gibson), yet it acts as a separate optimization step requiring an additional ~0.96s latency at the trajectory end.

Runtime and scalability constraints: on large-scale environments like LaMAR HGE, observation matching consumes ~0.88s per frame, limiting real-time performance unless observation frequency is reduced or grid resolution is coarsened.
